content: The review of the effectiveness of interventions for child maltreatment was inconclusive. None of the 40 studies included in the review specifically evaluated the impact of interventions on child abuse, neglect, or other adverse parenting outcomes. However, the review did identify positive effects on factors that are likely to protect against maltreatment, such as improved parenting knowledge, positive parenting practices, enhanced parent-child interactions, and reduced parental depression. Broader benefits were also observed in the domain of children’s socioemotional development, although findings related to child behavior problems were inconclusive. Moderation analyses revealed that some outcomes showed stronger effects in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). The interventions were found to be equally effective for children under and over one year of age, for parents participating in short-term (<12 months) or long-term (>12 months) interventions, and regardless of whether the interventions were delivered individually, in group formats, or in a combination of formats. They were also effective across various settings, including homes, community centers, and healthcare facilities. An updated review of early childhood development (ECD) interventions identified 11 additional studies conducted across three WHO regions. These included five trials in the African Region (Rwanda, Ethiopia, Zimbabwe), four in the Region of the Americas (Brazil, Chile, Colombia), and two in the Eastern Mediterranean Region (Pakistan). Sample sizes ranged from 25 to 1,613 participants, with the mean age of children at baseline between 1 and 25 months. Interventions were delivered either individually to parents or in parent groups, with the number of intended sessions ranging from 1 to 28. Evidence from the updated ECD review demonstrated beneficial effects on reducing violent disciplining in two studies, although one of these studies showed no effect at follow-up. Another study found an intervention to be effective in reducing negative disciplining practices, including harsh parenting. One additional study assessed child maltreatment as evaluated by social workers, but no cases of abuse or neglect were detected in either the intervention or control groups. Most studies reported positive effects on parenting practices and parental mental health. Moderator analyses from the larger LMIC effectiveness review indicated that intervention effects, including those on maltreatment, were consistent across preschool-aged children (mean age 2–5 years) and older children. Across all age groups (2–17 years), the data suggested that effects were consistent across universal, selective, and indicated prevention programs targeting varying levels of maltreatment risk. Some studies on parenting interventions explicitly referenced child or human rights concepts, while many others incorporated strategies aligned with child rights principles, such as teaching alternatives to harsh discipline and promoting respectful, collaborative approaches to working with parents. Parenting interventions were generally found to be socially acceptable across diverse communities and delivery staff globally. However, there is limited data on their sociocultural acceptability among adolescents or other stakeholder groups, including the general public. There is little evidence to suggest that factors such as poverty, low parental education, or child age and gender are associated with poorer intervention outcomes. Thus, parenting programs are unlikely to exacerbate existing inequities. At the family level, parents who participated in parenting programs rarely viewed them as stigmatizing. Instead, they valued the non-judgmental and empathetic approach of the delivery staff. Some studies indicated that attending parenting programs could shift parental norms regarding physical punishment and enhance social cohesion among parents participating in group formats. Financial analyses from the LMIC effectiveness review reported plausible program costs, ranging from $30 for a two-session program in Iran to $500 for a 14-session program in South Africa (median cost $55, based on 2015 prices). These costs were generally lower than those reported in high-income countries. However, no evidence was found on the broader economic impact of parenting interventions. Parenting interventions have been shown to be feasible to implement in various countries and effective in many randomized trials conducted in real-world service settings. While there are examples of interventions being scaled up in high-income countries, fewer examples exist in LMICs. Challenges to scaling up include political will, funding, workforce capacity, maintaining fidelity over time, and establishing governance systems for program sustainability. Planning for scale-up from the outset is critical to overcoming these challenges. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) identified several research gaps, including the need for further evaluation studies across diverse populations, outcomes, and contexts. Specific areas requiring additional research include the effectiveness of parenting interventions for adolescents in LMICs, parents who have already maltreated their children, families in humanitarian settings, and families living in extreme poverty. There is also a need for more data on long-term intervention effectiveness, independent assessments of parenting and child behaviors, and the inclusion of other caregivers and child self-reported data where appropriate. Adaptation of parenting programs to local contexts is essential to ensure cultural relevance and participant engagement while preserving the core components that make the interventions effective. Acceptable adaptations include translating materials, modifying images and cultural references, and adding locally relevant content. However, reducing program duration, cutting key messages, or using inadequately trained staff are generally unacceptable adaptations. Implementation considerations include building national commitment, assessing needs, selecting evidence-based interventions, and preparing government action plans. Sustainable financial support and robust monitoring and evaluation systems are critical for successful implementation and scale-up.
